title: As States Lose OB-GYNs, Some Look To Limit Medical Malpractice Risk
summary: Since 2025, at least four states have enacted laws restricting medical malpractice lawsuits. Patient advocates warn that the laws impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth and often pass with little attention.
content: When Anyssa Zancanella’s water broke during a family vacation near Salt Lake City, she expected better care there than she could get back home in rural Rock Springs, Wyoming, where many patients are flown out for emergency treatment. Instead, a crisis unfolded. Staff kept raising her doses of Pitocin, a drug that strengthens contractions, while the fetal monitor recorded mounting distress: The baby wasn’t getting enough oxygen. It took nearly 12 hours for the then-19-year-old to get an emergency cesarean section after the monitor showed signs of fetal distress, according to court records. Azaylee, now 7, was born with brain damage, likely from a reduced supply of oxygen and blood flow during delivery, causing cognitive disabilities, according to her family’s complaint. Last year, a judge found Steward Health Care, a Dallas-based for-profit health system that owned the West Valley City, Utah, hospital at the time, liable for gross medical negligence — and awarded the family $951 million. Steward Health Care did not respond to a request for comment for this article. Medical malpractice lawsuits against OB-GYNs are common in the U.S. healthcare system — childbirth can carry high risk and serious consequences. As a result, medical malpractice insurance costs for OB-GYNs are higher than for other specialties. Hospital administrators repeatedly cite the costs of those lawsuits and medical liability premiums as a reason to close their labor and delivery units. So, in recent years, state lawmakers began turning to what they say is a solution: tougher limits on malpractice lawsuits. Since 2025, at least four states, including Oklahoma , have enacted restrictions on medical malpractice suits. Utah added protections shielding physicians’ personal assets . New Mexico capped punitive damages , which punish wrongdoing beyond financial losses, and raised the standard of proof, requiring “clear and convincing” evidence for punitive damages. And Arkansas shortened the window a patient can file those suits after delivery. Anyssa Zancanella and her family vacation on the Oregon Coast. The family was awarded nearly $1 billion from a lawsuit over birth injuries to eldest daughter Azaylee (left). The reduced supply of oxygen and blood flow during her delivery caused Azaylee cognitive disabilities, according to the family’s complaint. (Esther Libby) The laws often pass with little fanfare, and patient advocates warn they impose more of a burden on families harmed during childbirth, many of whom don’t realize for years that they’ve been survivors of medical malpractice. “You really don’t know what you need to be looking for. You just know that you’re hurting,” said Deirdre Dickson-Gilbert, founder and national director of the National Medical Malpractice Advocacy Association . “And by the time you find out, the statutes of limitation are over with.” Other critics say the actions ignore alternative ways to retain obstetricians, such as addressing abortion bans, which several states pursued in this month’s midterm elections. In Virginia, for one, voters approved a constitutional amendment that not only protects abortion rights but bars the state from prosecuting physicians who perform the procedure. Missouri voters upheld abortion rights in their state constitution, and Nevada voters added them. But in deep-red Idaho, which had lost more than a third of its OB-GYNs two years after its near-total abortion ban took effect in 2022, voters rejected a proposal to restore access to the procedure. That left in place a law putting doctors at risk of prison time for providing a pregnant patient with lifesaving care. Obstetricians Leave States With Abortion Bans Since the U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, many OB-GYNs have left states with abortion bans, deepening maternity care shortages. States that restrict abortion, such as Alabama, Arkansas, and Idaho, are among those with the fewest maternity care providers relative to their population of women of reproductive age. In 2025, Arkansas limited malpractice claims stemming from childbirth to five years; other claims involving children can still be filed until a minor’s 11th birthday or two years post-injury, whichever is later. “A lot of these small rural hospitals will tell you they can’t afford to recruit OBs,” said Arkansas Rep. Aaron Pilkington, a Republican who co-sponsored that legislation. “Whatever you can do to just decrease the cost in recruiting them and paying for that malpractice insurance for a little bit, you know, to us, it was a worthwhile pursuit.” Combined with low Medicaid reimbursements and the 24/7 staffing required for obstetrics, labor and delivery units strain rural hospitals already on thin operating margins , according to the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, a policy center that tracks rural hospital closures. The group has counted at least 146 hospitals that have stopped delivering babies or plan to stop from the end of 2020 through this year. The Trump administration’s Medicaid cuts through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act added strain, since Medicaid covered roughly 40% of births in 2024 . Most cuts won’t take full effect until 2027 or later, but some hospitals have already cited them in closing labor and delivery units. “We’re seeing practices bought up by private equity and hospital systems because there are these compounding financial pressures on practices,” said Rachel Gandell Tetlow, vice president of government and political affairs for the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists. The group supported the medical malpractice bill that became law in New Mexico. In Monticello, Arkansas, the Mainline Health Monticello Clinic can be packed with pregnant patients by morning. Some drive more than an hour for their appointments. The clinic provides prenatal care for patients planning to deliver at Baptist Health Medical Center-Drew County, the county’s only birthing hospital. Since 2019, the clinic has absorbed extra patients as two other obstetrics units closed in neighboring counties in southeastern Arkansas. Fewer than a third of the state’s counties had a birthing hospital as of July, according to the policy nonprofit Arkansas Center for Health Improvement. Unlike many clinics, Monticello, as a federally qualified health center, is protected by the Federal Tort Claims Act from many medical malpractice claims. Lobbying groups, including the American Academy of Family Physicians and the National Association of Community Health Centers, have pushed Congress to extend the act to rural hospitals, so far without success. The Mainline Health Monticello Clinic in Arkansas can be packed with pregnant patients by morning. The clinic provides prenatal care for patients planning to deliver at Baptist Health Medical Center-Drew County, the county’s only birthing hospital. (Mainline Health Systems) Pilkington expects the law limiting malpractice claims will help other rural hospitals retain and staff their delivery units. He said Arkansas has had only one birth injury lawsuit in the past 10 years, which is why he believed the law wouldn’t significantly burden patients. State Rep. Ashley Hudson, a Democrat who co-sponsored the bill, said she supported the measure because it expands maternal care provisions, such as new Medicaid coverage for prenatal services and remote monitoring, but was skeptical that limiting malpractice cases would help recruit healthcare workers. “We wonder why we can’t attract providers to come into the state,” Hudson said, all while passing laws “second-guessing” providers’ ability to treat their patients and decide whether they need an abortion. Arkansas prohibits abortion in nearly all cases except to save the pregnant patient’s life. Waiting for a Payout Joanne Doroshow, executive director of the Center for Justice & Democracy at New York Law School, acknowledged that liability insurance is a genuine cost for hospitals and doctors but said capping what patients can recover doesn’t lower those premiums. “We know what can actually help doctors with their insurance rates. It’s got nothing to do with stripping away the rights of patients,” she said. “It has to do with accountability through the regulatory system, through the government that oversees the insurance industry that is allowing these companies to be price gouging.” In Zancanella’s case, Utah’s cap didn’t stop her from receiving a massive verdict. The state has capped noneconomic damages in malpractice cases at $450,000 since 2010, but it does not cap punitive damages. Economic damages repay a patient’s measurable financial losses, such as medical bills and lost wages, while noneconomic damages compensate for harm that cannot be measured by a receipt, like pain, suffering, or disability. Punitive damages are different from both: Rather than compensating the patient for what they lost, they’re meant to punish a doctor or hospital for especially reckless or malicious conduct. Azaylee is nonverbal and has seizures, and Zancanella takes her to Salt Lake City monthly for specialized pediatric care. In the first five years of Azaylee’s life, Zancanella said, her medical bills exceeded $1 million. The nearly $1 billion judgment was entered by default after Steward Health Care withdrew from the case. While battling the family’s lawsuit, the health system filed for bankruptcy in 2024, owing far more than it could pay. Steward Health Care sold the hospital to CommonSpirit Health in May 2023, along with four other Utah hospitals. The West Valley City hospital, now named Holy Cross Hospital-Jordan Valley West, still offers labor, delivery, recovery, and postpartum care. The payout is being worked out in bankruptcy court. Zancanella’s family hasn’t received any money yet. But she said she’s not discouraged and still feels the verdict held the hospital accountable. That outcome is common, Doroshow said. Such verdicts are “rarely, if ever, being paid fully.” “This notion that hospitals are going under, or doctors are somehow going bankrupt because of jury awards,” she said, “that’s clearly not true.” KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF—an independent source of health policy research, polling, and journalism. title: When Disaster Strikes, Medicaid Work Rules Add Barriers for Potential Enrollees
summary: Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work requirements create barriers for those trying to recover from natural disasters.
content: PO‘IPŪ, Hawai‘i — A month after Hurricane Lowell hit the island of Kauaʻi, downed trees, construction crews, and damaged homes dotted the neighborhoods. At the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort, where over 100 workers were laid off, heaps of sand blanketed the grounds, and the drained pool’s concrete deck crumbled into the beach, just steps away from the ocean. On Kauaʻi, unemployment claims jumped from 69 before the September hurricane to about 1,800 nearly two weeks afterward, with widespread layoffs in the tourism industry amid a sharp decline in visitors . The number of Medicaid applications submitted by island residents jumped by about 50% in the following month, according to the Hawaiʻi Department of Human Services. In times of emergencies, Medicaid provides a critical safety net for people to maintain healthcare coverage. But new work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed last year, have put Medicaid enrollees living in disaster-struck counties at risk of losing health insurance. The law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or attend school at least 80 hours a month, with eligibility checks starting in January. In most states, residents impacted by a disaster can be granted a short-term exemption from Medicaid work requirements. Eligibility largely relies on a federal law that allows the president to issue a disaster or emergency declaration and authorizes federal assistance, but any declaration can take months or may not come at all. Those who live in counties affected by natural disasters may not need to comply with the work rules — one of several carve-outs intended to provide limited, short-term exceptions. However, it’s unclear whether those who lost jobs after Hurricane Lowell would be eligible for that exemption so many months later. The Trump administration hasn’t offered clear guidance on how long a state can apply the natural disaster exemption to enrollees. Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, and her boyfriend were laid off by Sheraton and are getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. The union that represents the hotel’s hospitality workers secured them three months of health insurance. If Ganotisi isn’t hired back to her housekeeping job by then, she plans to apply for Medicaid, the federal-state program that provides health coverage to people with low incomes or disabilities. Rochelle Ganotisi, a mother of five, was laid off by the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort after it sustained significant damage from Hurricane Lowell. Her family is getting by with unemployment payments and part-time work. (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News) Hawaiʻi Gov. Josh Green, a Democrat and practicing physician, emphasized the importance of quickly issuing disaster declarations, especially as changes to Medicaid are set to take effect. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services allowed states to delay enforcing the work requirements until next July, but states are still expected to implement eligibility checks by Jan. 1. “It would be devastating if suddenly 40,000 or 50,000 people didn’t have their Medicaid benefits,” he said. “It could affect our rural hospitals, our nurse practitioners, our doctors, so timeliness is key.” Hawaiʻi officials said they will keep people who don’t meet the work requirements enrolled until July. Your browser does not support the audio element. Can’t see the audio player? Visit kffhealthnews.org to listen. At least 34 states, plus Washington, D.C., plan to adopt the optional hardship exemptions to those work requirements. So far, four states — Indiana, Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio — do not plan to adopt the exemptions, according to KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. All four were issued disaster declarations for severe storms and flooding this summer. CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster told KFF Health News in a statement that states can request a longer duration for a hardship exemption if they can prove that barriers to demonstrating work requirements persist in disaster areas. Tom Cotter, CEO of Health Response Alliance, a nonprofit focused on improving healthcare access in disasters, said that when people lose coverage they end up using emergency rooms and charitable clinics, among the few places that will treat patients regardless of their ability to pay. “All of these are really stretched thin during an emergency because their patient load goes way up,” he said. “That makes it even more expensive for the healthcare system that is being otherwise also burdened for the disaster.” With additional work requirements, “it is going to slow the economic recovery of any particular community,” Cotter said. “It’s going to require people to be thinking about how they’re paying for healthcare when they have a lot of other things to worry about.” Nebraska Work Requirements Begin Once the president declares a disaster or emergency, the short-term hardship exception applies for the full month the disaster took place . Eligibility can apply retroactively after a disaster declaration, and enrollees can be reimbursed for expenses from previous months. Nebraska implemented Medicaid work requirements early, in May, offering states a preview of how the hardship declaration might provide relief. For Nebraskans, that relief was delayed. It took three months for Trump to declare a federal disaster for March and April wildfires . For severe storms, tornadoes, and flooding that occurred in May, he didn’t declare a federal disaster until August . Six Nebraskans impacted by the disasters lost coverage because they did not comply with work requirements. In October, the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services reported it was reprocessing their eligibility now that they qualify for a hardship exemption. Sarah Maresh, director of the Health Care Access program at the nonprofit advocacy group Nebraska Appleseed, said the early rollout of the Medicaid work requirements has been marred by uncertainty. “This is part of the confusion that comes with the Medicaid work requirements, because it applies differently depending on your situation,” she said. “I think it’ll be very challenging for new applicants.” Local economies and businesses can take years to recover after a natural disaster. About 90% of businesses fail within two years after being struck by disaster, according to the U.S. Small Business Administration. Housing shortages can hamper business recovery as employees repair their homes or are displaced to areas farther from work. Three years after the 2023 Maui wildfires that killed over 100 people, recovery is ongoing , with most storefronts still shuttered in what was once a bustling area. After CMS published rules governing the exceptions to the work requirements, several Democratic states sued the agency. Their lawsuit cited the narrow time frame for securing natural disaster exceptions. The complaint argued that the lack of guidance burdens state Medicaid agencies determining eligibility. In its response filing , CMS wrote that the restrictions ensure the exemption applies only when a disaster affects Medicaid enrollees’ ability to comply with work requirements. Construction crews lined the roads on Kauaʻi a month after Hurricane Lowell, clearing debris and repairing damaged businesses, homes, and infrastructure. (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News) Disaster Delays, Denials In Trump’s second term, he has denied nearly a quarter of disaster and emergency declaration requests as of mid-November, a denial rate higher than that of any other presidential administration in more than two decades, KFF Health News found. While decision wait times have increased across the country, they’re more acute in states with Democratic governors. Those states experienced both significantly higher denial rates and longer decision times than states with Republican governors, according to 2026 analyses from The Associated Press and Politico’s E&E News . White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied any politicization in Trump’s decisions on disaster relief. She wrote that his response to requests from states ensures appropriate use of taxpayer money and that federal funds are used to “supplement — not substitute” states’ obligations to respond to disasters. The presidential major disaster declaration for Kauaʻi was the state’s sixth disaster or emergency declaration this year. As of November, Hawaiʻi had received more disaster and emergency declarations than any other state in 2026. Trump’s disaster declaration for a 6.0-magnitude earthquake that damaged over 300 homes on Hawaiʻi Island took about three months . The presidential major disaster declaration for Kauaʻi was the state’s sixth presidential disaster or emergency declaration this year — the most of any state so far in 2026. (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News) Piles of sand on the grounds of the Sheraton Kauaʻi Resort in the aftermath of Hurricane Lowell. (Ashley Mizuo/KFF Health News) Other states have waited longer for disaster declarations. New Mexico, where the Democratic Party controls the governor’s office and majorities in both legislative chambers, had one of the longest wait times for a decision — nine months for a presidential disaster declaration for severe storms and flooding in September 2025. Illinois, which also has a Democratic trifecta, waited over seven months and was denied. The state has yet to secure any major disaster declarations during Trump’s second term, despite several attempts . Some who lost their jobs and don’t qualify for Medicaid have few resources to help them. Oscar Cardova worked at The Terrace Hanalei, a restaurant on Kauaʻi’s North Shore that was significantly damaged in the hurricane. When the restaurant closed, he lost his employer-provided health insurance. Although he has a work permit visa from Peru, he was denied Medicaid because of his immigration status. Cardova and his wife, Yesenia, live in their van. Yesenia has astigmatism and, without insurance, she will need to pay for glasses out-of-pocket, Cardova said. The cost is expected to be about $500. The couple planned to work for two more years in the U.S. before returning to Peru. A month after the hurricane, they were still struggling to find work. In search of more job opportunities, they considered moving to Honolulu. “Right now, we’re just surviving,” Cardova said. “We’re waiting to see what happens before making other decisions, because we can’t keep living like this.” Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity?
